title: Buy vs. build is now also a UX decision, especially in enterprise
text:
Buy vs. build is now also a UX decision, especially in enterprise

Artificial intelligence made building cheap and buying easy. The trade-off now turns on who owns the upkeep, the seams between tools, the chat surfaces, and the data.

For most of my career, product management owned buy versus build. A product manager wrote the case, finance checked the math, and procurement signed.

Designers arrived after the decision was made, inherited whatever won, and spent years sanding its rough edges. Artificial intelligence changed the math on both sides at once.

Build is cheaper now, but the yearly upkeep never shows up in the business case.

Buy comes with legacy, and that legacy now includes someone else’s model, roadmap, and release calendar. And usually there’s a third option nobody names: replacing the system you already have.

Menlo Ventures found in 2025: The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise that 76% of enterprise artificial intelligence use cases were purchased rather than built, up from 53% a year earlier. Meanwhile, coding agents make a working internal tool look like an afternoon project.

More work happens inside Teams, Slack, Claude, and ChatGPT, surfaces neither option owns.

Don’t ask which option costs less, Ask where the complexity lands: in your code, in a vendor’s roadmap, or on your users.

Budget for Build Maintenance

A designer with a coding agent can now stand up an internal tool before a vendor’s sales team returns the call. Andrej Karpathy named that loose style vibe coding in 2025, and Simon Willison drew the line in Not all AI-assisted programming is vibe coding (but vibe coding rocks). Prototypes can be loose, but code you keep has to be read like any other.

Most internal tools become code you keep, which makes them products. It needs a budget, an owner, and someone to call when it breaks. Most teams don’t think of it that way, because nobody bought anything.

I learned this the hard way.

We built an internal workflow application in one place I worked at, before AI, because nothing we could buy matched how our teams worked. It shipped fast, people came to depend on it, and that’s exactly when it became a nightmare to maintain.

Every new approval step meant changing code few people understood, small fixes broke things elsewhere, and nobody had budgeted time for any of it.

That’s where my rule comes from. I budget 30% of the upfront build cost every year for upkeep: updates, patches, model changes, and new requests.

Run that math and many vibe-coded apps cost more than the subscriptions they replace. Say two people spend two weeks at a fully loaded $150 an hour, which is $24,000 up front and $7,200 a year after. A subscription at $20 a seat for 25 people runs $6,000 a year. Over three years, the build costs $45,600 against $18,000, and only one of them came with a support team.

Every generated line is a line somebody has to own, and the initial owner usually doesn’t want that responsibility.

Open source taught this lesson first. Black Duck’s 2026 Open Source Security and Risk Analysis Report found open source in 98% of audited codebases, and 93% held components with no development activity in two years.

In 2024, a backdoor reached the widely used XZ Utils library after an attacker spent years earning its maintainer’s trust. Generated code has the same weakness: nobody paid for it, so nobody budgeted to watch it. Google’s 2025 DORA Report found adoption of artificial intelligence still hurts delivery stability.

Accept the Vendor’s Legacy

Buying looks like the cautious choice, and often it is.

Purchases from specialized vendors succeeded about 67% of the time, while internal builds succeeded about a third as often, according to research from MIT’s NANDA initiative covered in Fortune’s MIT report: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing.

The fair objection is selection, since companies tend to buy for well-understood problems and build for messy ones, which flatters vendors. Hold the number loosely, but the direction matches where enterprise budgets went.

A purchase is never only a feature set. You also get the vendor’s data model, release cadence, and theory of what your users are trying to do.

When you buy, you import another company’s organization chart.

Systems mirror the communication structures of the organizations that design them, as Melvin Conway observed in 1968. Your users end up inside a product tuned for that company’s largest customers, who may look nothing like yours.

Measure the Tool Gaps

Users don’t experience your build or your purchase on its own. They experience the gaps. You can count those gaps the way you’d count clicks in a usability test: pick one real task, follow it across systems, and log every switch and every retyped value.

The gaps add up fast.

People in a 2022 study of 137 workers on 20 teams at three Fortune 500 companies switched between applications and websites roughly 1,200 times a day. Reorienting after each switch cost them just under four hours a week, about 9% of their working time, according to How Much Time and Energy Do We Waste Toggling Between Applications? in Harvard Business Review and AAPL Leadership.

Homegrown tools widen the gaps too. In the 1990s, departments built their own Microsoft Access databases because waiting on the central technology team took a quarter.

The databases worked until their authors changed jobs, and then the data inside them became one more place nobody could reach. Today’s version is drift: patterns that stop matching the rest of the product and error states nobody designed.

Complexity always lands somewhere, and the only choice is where.

Complexity is conserved, and the only real choice is who absorbs it. That’s Larry Tesler’s law.

A build moves complexity into your codebase, while a purchase moves it into someone else’s roadmap. A careless mix of both moves it onto your users, one copy-and-paste at a time. Before anyone argues about license fees, ask where the complexity ends up under each option.

Design for Host Surfaces

In many organizations, the place people meet your product is no longer your product. It’s Teams, Slack, Claude, or ChatGPT.

Apps moved inside ChatGPT conversations in 2025 with OpenAI’s Introducing apps in ChatGPT and the new Apps SDK. In January 2026, MCP Apps — Bringing UI Capabilities To MCP Clients let tools return interactive interfaces that render inside Claude and ChatGPT. Build or buy, your most-used screen may end up as a card in someone else’s window.

I’ve worked inside this arrangement before. I designed the developer documentation site for Myspace, whose 2008 developer platform let third-party applications run on member profiles. The host set the box size, the permissions, and what an app could know about the person looking at it. Every app was designed inside that frame, and chat surfaces are drawing it again.

The host draws the frame, and your job is deciding what fits inside it.

The rules are specific, and they belong to the host. An inline card in ChatGPT gets at most two actions, no nested scrolling, the system font, and a logo the host adds for you, per OpenAI’s UI guidelines for the Apps SDK.

A Slack message holds up to 50 blocks under Block Kit. Microsoft’s Types of Cards & their Usage names Adaptive Cards the recommended card type for new Teams development.

People expect your product to work like the places where they spend most of their time, which is Jakob Nielsen’s Jakob’s Law of Internet User Experience. Inside a chat surface, that stops being advice, because the host’s patterns are the only ones on offer. So design the card as its own product, with one job, one primary action, and a handoff to your full application when the task outgrows it.

Count the Replacement Cost

Most of these decisions aren’t made on empty ground. Something already exists, and the real question is whether to replace it. Replacement carries costs that appear in neither column.

The first cost is lost expertise. Task time falls with repetition, which is the Power Law of Practice covered on my UX Guidelines site (@usabilitycounts), and your power users have years of repetitions in the old tool. Replace it, and they start the curve over, usually in the busiest quarter.

The second cost is hidden rules. You shouldn’t tear down a fence until you know why it went up, as G. K. Chesterton argued in 1929. Old enterprise software is full of fences, and each one was a rule somebody once needed.

The new thing always wins the demo against the tool people already know.

The third cost is our own bias. People value their amateur work about as highly as experts’ work, according to Michael Norton and his co-authors in The IKEA Effect: When Labor Leads to Love. Melissa Perri described the organizational version in The Build Trap: building is the easy part, and teams get rewarded for shipping instead of for learning what customers need.

Not invented here makes it worse. Not invented here is the reflex of rejecting an outside solution because someone else made it. Ralph Katz and Thomas Allen tracked 50 research and development project groups for An empirical test of the Not Invented Here (NIH) Syndrome, a 1980 MIT working paper.

Groups that had worked together five or more years performed significantly worse, and they talked less with professionals outside the team. Coding agents lower the price of acting on that reflex, because rebuilding a vendor’s feature now takes a weekend instead of a budget cycle.

Coding agents also distort the estimate. Experienced developers took 19% longer on real tasks with the tools, yet estimated afterward they had been 20% faster, in METR’s randomized trial Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity.

It’s one study of 16 developers, and METR now flags it as out of date. Still, price your own prototype the way you’d price a stranger’s.

Buy Commodities, Build Differentiators

The clearest test I know comes from Simon Wardley (@swardley). In Finding a path, he sorts components from genesis to custom built to product to commodity.

His shorthand for building commodities yourself is Thomas Thwaites, the designer who spent nine months trying to build a toaster from raw materials. A coding agent shrinks the nine months to a weekend, which matters less than it seems, because you still own every repair after it ships.

Coding agents change the toaster math, not the toaster.

For products built on artificial intelligence, the map has a clear split. The model is sliding toward commodity, rented by the token. The experience around it is still custom: how a suggestion explains itself, how someone corrects it, and whether people trust it. A competitor can’t copy that by signing the same contract.

Building still wins in a few places. Build when your own data is the advantage and a vendor would have to hold it to use it.

Build when regulation rules out every product on the market, and build the moments you compete on. If a feature would look the same in every competitor’s product, though, it’s probably a commodity.

Those cases also assume you have the people, and most organizations don’t. Vibe coding gets you a demo, not the skills a production artificial intelligence application needs: retrieval over messy records, evaluations, permissions, and monitoring.

IBM surveyed 8,584 technology professionals for Data Suggests Growth in Enterprise Adoption of AI is Due to Widespread Deployment by Early Adopters, published in January 2024. Limited skills and expertise topped the barriers at 33%, with data complexity next at 25%. The more data an application touches, the wider that gap gets.

Map Where Data Lives

A model can only answer from what it can see, so the experience follows wherever your data lives. Buy a tool and your records sit in the vendor’s schema, reachable on the vendor’s terms.

Build one and the data stays yours, along with the job of governing it. When Anthropic announced the Model Context Protocol in 2024, it described models cut off from data trapped behind silos and legacy systems.

So run the landing test a second time, aimed at the data. A card in Teams is only as useful as the permissions behind it, and an assistant that can’t reach the contract can’t summarize it.

Whoever holds the records decides what any surface can show.

Regulation is starting to price this in. The law has applied since September 12, 2025, and switching charges between data processing providers, including data egress fees, end entirely on January 12, 2027, according to the European Commission’s Data Act explained.

Leaving a vendor is getting cheaper on paper. In practice, a migration is mostly a data project with a UX bill attached: renamed fields, lost history, and reports that no longer match.

Before any contract, ask where the data will live, who can export it and in what format, and whether the surfaces your people already use can reach it.

Those answers shape the experience more than the feature list does.

Prepare for Model Retirement

Either way, part of your product now runs on something you don’t control. Build on a model and that model will be retired. Anthropic promises at least 60 days’ notice before retiring a publicly released model.

Its Model deprecations page lists the Claude Sonnet 4.5 snapshot from September 2025 as deprecated on September 30, 2026, with retirement set for November 30, 2026.

Buy a product built on a model and the same thing happens, one layer removed and on the vendor’s schedule. Tone shifts. Refusals move. Summaries grow or shrink, and edge cases that used to pass start failing. A vendor’s release notes may not mention a model change at all, so ask in the contract how much notice you’ll get.

A model swap is a redesign nobody scheduled, and now happens on a frequent basis. Maintenane is now a real time activity.

The exit plan belongs to design, not only to procurement. Keep a set of real user tasks with known good outcomes, run them against every new model or vendor release, and review the results the way you’d review a usability study. Twenty or thirty tasks is enough to start, as long as they include the common requests, the expensive mistakes, and the cases where the correct response is to decline.

Decide Where Complexity Lands

Buy versus build used to end at the signature or at launch. Now neither choice finishes, because the parts keep moving after the decision. Building got cheaper and stayed expensive to own. Buying got easier and arrived carrying more of someone else’s history than the demo let on.

So the decision can’t stay with product management and finance. The numbers in that spreadsheet are real enough. They just leave out the costs users feel most: drift in tools nobody maintains, expertise lost when an old system goes away, data stuck where new tools can’t reach it, and chat surfaces whose layout rules you don’t set.

Designers, product managers, and researchers are the people who see those costs first. They can also measure them, in task time and in the moments where someone gives up. Bring that evidence to the decision before it’s made, not after it ships.

The landing test won’t tell you whether to buy or build. It tells you where the complexity will go, so somebody can be standing there on purpose. Most of the time, that points toward buying the commodity and building the difference. The seams between the two are yours either way, so design them.

Action Items

  • Test vendors against prototypes. Run a hands-on bake-off with real tasks, using the scenario-based method in The Right Way to Select Technology by Tony Byrne and Jarrod Gingras. Enter your current system and a quick internal prototype alongside the vendors, and ask the current system’s heaviest users why each odd step exists.
  • List every system touched. Pick one real task and follow it from start to finish. Write down each system it passes through, where each value is stored, and who can export it, then put that list in the business case next to the license fee.
  • Budget 30% for upkeep. Before a build ships, name the person who maintains it and set aside 30% of its build cost every year. Treat that line as fixed, the way you would a subscription, so fixes and library updates don’t wait for spare time.
  • Retest after model changes. Keep 20 to 30 real tasks with known good answers, including the common requests and the costly mistakes. Run them whenever a model or vendor release changes what’s underneath, and review the results like a usability study.

Buy vs. build is now also a UX decision, especially in enterprise was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: A founder with a tool is not a founder with a clue
text:
A founder with a tool is not a founder with a clue

AI lets a solo founder produce a product, but it can’t help them understand whether that product is actually good…yet. That expertise, the hard-won judgment underneath it, has always been what decides who wins and who quietly (or epically) fails.

There’s a movement in the startup world that currently claims if you can’t build your product by yourself, with AI, you shouldn’t be building it at all. The “advice” suggests that a solo founder should handle coding, design, and marketing with AI and should not hire a traditional team at all.

Hiring someone to design or engineer your product, whether it’s an agency, a contractor, or an early employee, is treated as proof you don’t really understand your own product and a growing number of investors won’t back a founder who would do that.

Most founders are doing exactly what they’ve been told works, and often they don’t know any better. The idea that needing help is a weakness sets a tone that will eventually backfire because most people are not unicorns, because unicorns do not exist.

Paul Graham, who founded Y Combinator, has said for years that he prefers founders who can build the thing themselves. Carles Reina, an early backer of ElevenLabs, told CNBC his first instant red flag is a founder who “literally cannot build products.” More than a third of new startups are now solo-founded, because AI made it possible to go from idea to working product without the people who used to be required.

Buried in that whole position is an assumption that’s dangerously misguided. It assumes that because you can now produce the thing, you have the expertise to know whether the thing is any good. Those have never been the same thing.

AI collapsed the cost of making something to almost nothing, but it did nothing to impact the cost of judgment, the years of studying how people behave, what makes a product feel trustworthy.

We got product creation for free, but forgot that expertise didn’t come with it.

Being able to vibe-code an app over a weekend makes you an expert in exactly one thing. Can you guess? It’s in vibe-coding an app over a weekend.

I lean on these tools as hard as anyone, on fast, super AI-heavy schedules that pressure test the technology every day. Even at that speed, it’s obvious how often what comes out is close but not right, and how often it takes real experience and hard-won knowledge to catch the difference and make the call.

None of this is a knock on the founders who build a product themselves. Seriously, kudos to them. A founder who vibe-codes their idea into something real is doing something genuinely good, they’re getting what’s in their head out into the world, fast, and that has always been the hard part.

The trouble starts when the people funding them treat that first draft as the finished product, and think asking for help is a weakness.

AI moves the thinking rather than removing it. The people cheering the death of the expert have confused two different things, making what you asked for, and knowing whether what got made is any good.

Where they’re right

Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, the company behind Claude, has said he thinks the first billion-dollar company run by a single person could arrive as soon as 2026, and he put the odds at something like seventy to eighty percent. He has an obvious stake in that being true and his company creates tools that would make it possible, but nevertheless, the prediction could be realistic.

Venture capitalist and Harvard Business School professor, Jeff Bussgang, has described the same shift from the investing side, right down to a betting pool among his tech-CEO friends over the year the first one-person billion-dollar company shows up.

The cost of producing software, a brand, a marketing campaign, a working prototype, has fallen through the floor. A founder with the right AI stack can now do in a weekend what used to take a team a quarter.

Andreessen Horowitz says that building has gotten so cheap that founders now skip the questions they used to have to answer first. Their Speedrun team’s perspective is that the interesting question is no longer “can you build it,” because the answer is now always yes. The interesting, and perhaps more important question is “should you,” which is what it’s always been. Marty Cagan has been telling product teams for decades that the job is to ask not just whether you can build the thing, but whether you should build it at all.

When making the thing is nearly free, the discipline shifts from execution to judgment about what deserves to exist at all.

The money has unsurprisingly moved accordingly. At TechCrunch Disrupt, seed investors including Elizabeth Yin urged early-stage founders to lean on AI coding leverage as much as they can, and Renata Quintini of Renegade Partners agreed it’s the right move for finding product-market fit, rather than spending early cash on headcount they don’t yet need.

Rebecca Lynn points out that it’s never been easier to stand up a company “in demo mode,” which is exactly why she’s careful about what she funds.

The thing these investors are reacting to is that a lot of the roles that used to be mandatory at the start of a company are now optional, or at least deferrable.

Startups have a long history of getting too big, too early. The Startup Genome Report, which analyzed more than 3,200 startups, found that premature scaling, hiring too many people too soon is the single most common reason startups fail.

Starting with a small team is generally smarter, but a founder who can build the first version themselves, who understands the problem because they live it, who doesn’t need to hire a translator to turn their idea into a thing, has a real and durable advantage.

The clearest case is the technical founder building for people exactly like themselves, the engineer making tools for engineers, who is both the builder and the user and genuinely doesn’t need anyone in between.

The trend is shifting to the founder building it alone, but the reality is they often shouldn’t.

Travis Howell and Todd Hall looked at whether solo founders can hold their own against co-founded teams, and found that they can, under one condition, when the solo founder has deep, broad experience to draw on.

It works when the founder’s real expertise is in building the thing, the craft, the risks, the details that make a product good, not just in the problem it solves. A technical founder building for engineers can do it, because what they know maps onto what the product needs.

Knowing an industry cold, or a market, or a customer, is valuable, but it is not the same as knowing how to build something people want to use.

Right now, the industry keeps confusing the two. Thinking a tool will fix it is just foolish.

Telling a founder that reaching out for help, from someone who could genuinely add qualified perspective or experience, is a red flag gets it backwards. It punishes a person for not personally holding every bit of knowledge a company needs, which is a bar no real human should be held to.

Eight people in a conference room

On a Saturday morning in 1999, five of us met at iXL’s offices in Manhattan’s Union Square to stage a quiet coup. We picked the day on purpose. The place was empty, no account directors, really nobody around to hear what we were about to do. Just us gathered around a table voluntarily sequestered in a conference room to discuss a project we thought we could save by making it smaller.

iXL was one of those agencies that got enormous by swallowing other agencies, which is what was common during dot-com 1.0. Agency size wasn’t a virtue or a sin, it was just the reality of the industry. The project we were on had at least forty people attached to it, with one of the largest budgets in the company, and it was sinking under its own weight.

There was too much process, too many people who had to be looped in before decisions could be made, a launch date that kept on sliding.

This wasn’t a new phenomenon (not that I knew that at the time). In 1975, computer scientist Fred Brooks watched IBM try to rescue a late software project by adding programmers, and watched it get later. He turned it into Brooks’s Law, which says that adding people late to a project just makes it even later.

It’s a brutal, mathematical reality. As you add people, each new person you add has to be brought up to speed, which pulls the people who already know what they’re doing away from the work. Every new person adds a communication line to every other person, so the coordination cost climbs faster than the output does.

Forty people don’t move four times faster than ten. They move slower, they cause blockers left and right, but they feel busier doing it.

We wanted to cut the team to eight, with severe focus. Eight specialists, each the best in the building at one specific thing. The cast list we wanted:

  • A front-end developer
  • A couple of back-end developers
  • A project manager
  • An information architect (which is what you called a UX designer back then)
  • An art director
  • A creative director
  • A designer

The premise wasn’t to fire the other forty members of the team. They’d have plenty of work to do on what was next on the roadmap, but to actually ship this thing, we needed the smallest possible group of people who each could use their expertise to collaborate and move this forward smarter and faster.

Years later, Amazon would make this famous as the two-pizza team, Jeff Bezos’s rule that no team should be bigger than two pizzas can feed, somewhere around ten people, because that’s the size that stays fast.

I was twenty-three. I was nowhere near the most senior person in that room, though I was somehow the most senior information architect on the project in all of New York, which should tell you how little a title and actual expertise have to do with each other.

I was also, for the record, a bit of a troublemaker, which is how you end up in an empty office on a Saturday trying to shrink your own project by eighty percent. We wrote the plan, we walked our account director through it, and somehow he said yes.

Then we had to go do it, and we did.

That little team became a precision instrument the company reached for whenever something hard had to get built fast, and I’m confident it made them a lot of money.

As for the giants that were busy getting bigger, most of them did not make it. iXL shrank drastically. MarchFirst, the largest of these roll-ups, a nine-thousand-person, six-billion-dollar web consultancy, burned through a billion and a half dollars in fourteen months and filed the biggest bankruptcy in the industry’s history.

The whole sector contracted by seventy to eighty percent. Being huge turned out to be the most expensive way to be fragile.

That is all to say, the idea of small, nimble teams is rarely a bad idea, so when a venture capitalist says a founder doesn’t need forty people, I can’t argue with that.

The thing to understand is the strategy of what we did in that room, because that is not the argument for the solo founder show being encouraged today.

We cut forty people down to eight experts. The pitch today is to cut it down to one founder and a tool. Those may sound similar, but one of them concentrates expertise, while the other removes it and hopes the software quietly fills the hole where it used to be.

Patrick Neeman argues that in the age of AI, when anyone can stand up the same model and the same features, the thing that sets your product apart is the experience and the judgment built around it. You own what differentiates you, the workflows, the design, the taste, the deep understanding of your user, and you buy or borrow the commodity underneath.

The mistake in the solo-founder pitch is assuming the tool handed you the part that differentiates. All it really handed you was a commodity.

Ethan Mollick, who is about as bullish on AI at work as anyone, insists that AI rewards expertise. It lets the people who already know what good looks like judge the output, catch the confident mistakes, and push the tool past its defaults, while everyone else takes whatever the machine hands them.

The AI builds you a slick dashboard and never thinks to ask what it looks like before there’s any data in it, or when something breaks. It gives you a clean screen with light gray text on white, and someone who knows catches that a lot of your users can’t read it. That stuff only gets caught when someone with real experience is deciding whether it’s actually done or even takes the time to ask the AI to review it.

Tao An, a researcher at Hawaii Pacific University, lays out the split cleanly, saying that on routine work, AI lifts a beginner up to a competent floor, which is real and useful. On the hard, judgment-heavy work, however, the kind that decides whether a product is actually good, it does the opposite. It widens the gap between the person who knows what they’re doing and the person who doesn’t, because only one of them can tell when the confident-looking answer is wrong.

The tool amplifies the expertise in the room. It does not supply it.

At the end of the day, this comes down to one thing: the expertise has to be in the room. An employee, a contractor, a cofounder, a partner, or you, if you genuinely have it. Assemble it however you want, and keep the team as small as the work allows. The tool will make almost anything you ask it to. What it cannot do is tell you whether the thing is any good. That part has always belonged to the people who know, and it still does.

The thing you can’t prompt

In 1986, Steve Jobs needed a logo for NeXT, the company he started after being pushed out of Apple. He hired Paul Rand, probably the most famous graphic designer alive, and asked him for a few options to choose from. Rand said no. He would solve the problem, he told Jobs, hand back a single answer and Jobs could take it or leave it.

He charged a hundred thousand dollars. He came back with one design, a black cube tilted at twenty-eight degrees, presented in a bound book that walked Jobs through every decision, why the word, why the lowercase “e,” why the angle, until the logo felt less like a choice and more like the only possible conclusion.

Jobs, who genuinely had plenty of taste himself, paid six figures for something he couldn’t produce on his own. Whatever was in his head, he could have generated a thousand tilted cubes before lunch, but the reasoning underneath that piece of design derived from years of accumulated judgment that let Rand know, with total confidence, which single answer was right and why.

This is the gap the whole “just build it yourself” argument ignores. Producing the deliverable (whatever it may be) and knowing whether the deliverable is good are completely different skills.

Right now, you can easily generate a logo, a landing page, an entire app, in an afternoon. What you cannot necessarily do is hold the judgment to look at what came out and know that the hierarchy is off, that the flow asks too much of a tired person, that the tone is wrong for the people you’re trying to reach, that the confident, finished-looking thing on your screen is quietly, expensively broken or costing you customers.

Christian Holst found that the average checkout asks for around eleven form fields when most need eight, and that nearly one in five people abandon a purchase simply because the process felt too long. In testing, cutting a form from eleven fields to four lifted completions by 120 percent. The tool that built you that form has no idea it’s costing you customers.

AI makes everything it spits out look “good.” It can be clean, modern, professional, but that’s not always a perk. It’s also pulling from the same places everyone else is pulling from. When everyone builds with the same tools, trained on the same examples, everything starts to look the same.

Aurelie Radom suggests that AI may not have democratized design judgment, but it did democratize output, and when the models are all trained on the same stuff, the output space compresses and products that have nothing to do with each other start converging on the same shapes and the same layouts.

Alwin de Rooij and Michael Mose Biskjaer compared nineteen studies around this and found the effect is real and very measurable. The more people lean on the same AI, the more their work converges, which means looking finished and modern is fast becoming the least distinctive thing a product can be.

Looking finished used to mean something, odds were decent that someone who knew what they were doing added a contextual lens. That’s not true anymore. AI gives you the finished look in seconds, whether or not a single smart decision went into it.

Humans, it turns out, are built to fall for this distraction. In 1995, Masaaki Kurosu and Kaori Kashimura put a set of interface layouts in front of people and found the better-looking ones got rated as easier to use, even when they flat-out weren’t. They called it the aesthetic-usability effect.

We see something attractive and our brain quietly decides it works.

AI produces attractive by default, which means it produces trust it hasn’t earned because the thing it created looks great, you believe it’s good, but there’s no proof it actually will work.

Fabrizio Dell’Acqua, Ethan Mollick, and their colleagues studied 758 consultants and found that on the tasks AI is bad at, the ones who relied on it did worse than the ones who didn’t. The AI gave them wrong answers that looked right, and the people who couldn’t tell the difference used them anyway.

Separately, Yue Liu and colleagues studied a large batch of AI-written code and found it full of quality and maintainability problems hiding under a finished surface.

This isn’t a secret in our field. Nicole Alexandra Michaelis calls it the “taste paradox,” where we all agree that knowing what’s good is the skill that matters most now, and we’ve built a way of working that keeps people from ever learning it. The more you lean on AI to tell you what works, the less you ever figure out how to tell on your own.

Ruiqi Zhou adds a business lens to this, saying that if everyone can make the same thing, making it isn’t an advantage anymore. The only thing still worth anything is the judgment to know what’s worth making.

The receipts

This isn’t an emotional argument about how things look. The numbers back it up. The business value of expertise is one of the most heavily documented things in product, and the data got sharper once AI showed up.

Hyunso Kim, Hyo Kang, and Jaeyong Song studied more than 160,000 product launches on Product Hunt, before and after ChatGPT arrived, and found that after AI showed up, solo launches spiked, especially in categories that used to require a team, but when they looked at quality, at which products actually reached the top tier, teams still dominated, as much as ever.

AI widened the door for solo entry and did nothing to close the quality gap. More things got made. The good things still came from the people with the expertise to make them good.

The money follows the same pattern. First Round Capital studied a decade of its own portfolio and found that companies with more than one founder outperformed solo founders by 163 percent, raised more, and grew faster, an advantage they tie directly to complementary skill and the sharper decisions it produces. Their data says the opposite of their advice.

That’s not a nostalgia story about the pre-AI days. Boston Consulting Group found that the companies leading in AI, the ones it calls “future-built,” are outgrowing their competitors by 1.7 times in revenue and 3.6 times in shareholder return.

These winners used real expertise to aim the new tools and didn’t just buy the tools to replace the expertise.

Benedict Sheppard, Hugo Sarrazin, Garen Kouyoumjian, and Fabricio Dore scored hundreds of companies on how seriously they treat design, then tracked their results over five years. The ones that took design most seriously grew revenue about a third faster than the ones that didn’t, and returned more than half again as much to their shareholders.

The same research shows why those winners are so rare. More than forty percent of companies still don’t talk to their users while they’re building, and over half have no real way to tell whether their own team’s work is any good.

Taking design seriously is what separates the winners from everyone else. Taking design seriously means being able to judge whether your design is actually working. Most companies can’t or just don’t.

If most companies can’t tell good design from bad in the first place, then of course they’ll believe AI made them something good. They have no way to know it didn’t.

Judgment is not the same as one powerful person’s gut, and the answer to “the tool can’t decide for you” is not “so let the loudest opinion in the room decide instead.” In 2009, Google’s lead designer Doug Bowman quit and explained why in a post called “Goodbye, Google.” The company, he wrote, couldn’t choose between two shades of blue, so it tested forty-one.

He’d been asked to prove, with data, whether a border should be three, four, or five pixels wide. That’s the opposite mistake, and it’s just as bad. When no one on the team can just say “four,” you test everything, because nobody has the expertise, trust or standing to make the call.

Real expertise is knowing which decisions you can settle and move on from in a second and which ones actually need testing.

Build small. Just bring the expertise.

Rick Rubin has produced some of the most important records of the last forty years, across rock, rap, country, and pop, with artists such as Johnny Cash, Jay-Z, the Red Hot Chili Peppers, and Adele.

When Anderson Cooper asked him, on 60 Minutes, whether he could play instruments or work a soundboard, Rubin said no. “I have no technical ability,” he said. “And I know nothing about music.”

Cooper, reasonably, asked what he was being paid for. Rubin’s answer sums up why an expert lens matters. He said, “The confidence that I have in my taste and my ability to express what I feel has proven helpful for artists.”

He can’t compose the tracks himself, but he is one of the most sought-after people in music anyway, because composition isn’t always the point. Judgment is.

The ability to sit with a thing and know, with conviction, what it needs and what’s getting in the way is the rarest and most valuable thing in any creative endeavor. It is exactly the thing that does not reside in a tool, no matter how good the tool gets.

The people telling founders they don’t need anyone but themselves and AI are half right in a way that matters. You certainly don’t need forty people. You may not even need ten. It’s fair to say that the bloat they’re concerned about is real, and killing that is good, but they’ve taken a true thing about team size and turned it into a false thing about expertise.

Fewer people, yes. Less expertise, no.

Right now, AI gives you the output of expertise without the expertise. It hands you the artifact a skilled person would have made, without the judgment that skilled person would use to know whether the artifact is any good.

That gap is real today, and it is real for the foreseeable future, though I won’t pretend to know how long “foreseeable” lasts. Maybe the models close it, maybe judgment turns out to be the last thing to automate.

Either way, you have to build in the world you’re actually in, and in this one, AI can make the thing, but it cannot tell you if the thing is good.

Founders actually doing this are the first to admit where it breaks. Anik Devaughn, who built an AI-native commerce platform largely by himself, said that founders who understand their business deeply can move faster and stay smaller, but the ones who can’t evaluate the work will just automate bad decisions.

Basically, if you’re a founder talking to an investor who says they won’t back anyone who hires help, the investor is missing the point.

A founder who can tell the difference between what’s working and what isn’t is a far safer bet than one who can only tell you the demo they put together looks great.

This is not an argument for hiring an agency, or hiring anyone in particular. It’s an argument for embracing the expertise that has to be there to create success. It can be an employee or a contractor, a cofounder or a partner, or you, if you’ve genuinely put in the years.

NYU Professor J.P. Eggers ran an experiment where MBA students used AI agents to build startups from scratch. The AI was good at discrete tasks and fast brainstorming, he found, but it couldn’t replace the judgment that comes from having real specialists in the room.

His line for what happens without them sums up a lot, saying “You’re kind of taking it on faith that what the AI is producing is pretty good.”

Assemble the smallest team you can. Keep it lean enough to move fast, and make sure someone on it can tell what’s right from what’s broken. AI can build anything. Knowing if it’s right takes a human.

AI or not, it all falls apart without someone who actually knows what they’re doing.

Anyone who treats a founder’s willingness to bring in that person as weakness has it backwards. A founder who knows what they don’t know, and goes and gets the help, is the one worth betting on.

References and further reading

The belief that you should build it yourself

  • Diana Bocco, AI Is Letting Solo Founders Build Startups Without Hiring (Inc.). The solo-founder-with-AI movement in the founders’ own words, including the line that founders who can’t evaluate the work just automate bad decisions.
  • Paul Graham, How to Start a Startup. The Y Combinator view that the best ideas are the ones founders can build themselves.
  • Carles Reina (CNBC). The ElevenLabs backer on why a founder who “literally cannot build products” is an instant red flag.
  • The State of Solo Founding (Carta data). More than a third of new startups are now solo-founded.

Where they’re right

  • Dario Amodei (Inc.). The Anthropic CEO’s prediction of the first one-person billion-dollar company by 2026.
  • Jeff Bussgang, AI and the Dawn of the 10x Founder. A VC and HBS professor on the same shift, and on AI multiplying expertise rather than replacing it.
  • a16z Speedrun, The Idiot Index for Code. Building got so cheap that the real question moved from “can you?” to “should you?”
  • Elizabeth Yin and Renata Quintini (TechCrunch). Seed investors on leaning into AI coding leverage at the earliest stage.
  • Rebecca Lynn (via MLnotes). On how easy it is to stand up a company “in demo mode,” and why that makes her cautious.
  • Startup Genome, Premature Scaling. Across 3,200+ startups, scaling too fast, hiring too many too soon, is the most common reason startups fail.
  • Travis Howell and Todd Hall, Lone Genius or Lonely Fool? (Strategic Management Journal). Solo founders can hold their own, but only when they personally carry deep, broad expertise.
  • Marty Cagan, Product Management: Start Here (SVPG). Decades of arguing that the job is to ask not just whether you can build it, but whether you should.

Small teams and the strategy of focus

  • iXL and MarchFirst (Unicorn Burn). The dot-com roll-up giants that grew huge and collapsed; MarchFirst burned through $1.5 billion in fourteen months.
  • Fred Brooks, Brooks’s Law. Adding people to a late project makes it later, because coordination cost climbs faster than output.
  • The Two-Pizza Team. Jeff Bezos’s rule that the fastest teams are small enough to feed with two pizzas.
  • Patrick Neeman, Buy Versus Build Is Now a UX Decision. Own the experience and judgment that set your product apart; buy or borrow the commodity underneath.
  • Ethan Mollick, The Cybernetic Teammate. AI rewards expertise: the people who know what good looks like get the most out of it.
  • Tao An (arXiv). On routine work AI lifts beginners up; on hard, judgment-heavy work it widens the gap between those who know and those who don’t.

Why output is not expertise

  • Christian Holst, Baymard Institute. The average checkout asks for more form fields than it needs; trimming them can lift completions by 120 percent.
  • Masaaki Kurosu and Kaori Kashimura, the aesthetic-usability effect. People rate better-looking interfaces as more usable, even when they aren’t.
  • Aurelie Radom, AI Made Everyone a Creator, Not a Designer. AI democratized output, not design judgment, so products that have nothing to do with each other keep converging on the same shapes and layouts.
  • Alwin de Rooij and Michael Mose Biskjaer, Does Generative AI Make Us Think Alike? A review of nineteen studies finding a real, measurable homogenization effect: the more people lean on the same AI, the more their work converges.
  • Fabrizio Dell’Acqua, Ethan Mollick, and colleagues (Harvard Business School). On tasks AI is bad at, consultants who leaned on it did worse, because it produced wrong answers that looked right.
  • Yue Liu and colleagues (arXiv). A large study of AI-written code found it full of quality and maintainability problems beneath a finished surface.
  • Nicole Alexandra Michaelis, The Taste Paradox. Everyone agrees judgment is the skill that matters most, and the current way of working keeps people from ever building it.
  • Ruiqi Zhou, Taste Is the New Moat, and That’s the Problem. If everyone can produce the output, the only thing left with value is the judgment to direct it.

The receipts

  • Hyunso Kim, Hyo Kang, and Jaeyong Song (arXiv). Across 160,000+ Product Hunt launches, AI boosted solo entry but quality still concentrated in teams.
  • First Round Capital, The 10-Year Project. Companies with more than one founder outperformed solo founders by 163 percent.
  • Boston Consulting Group, Build for the Future. Companies leading in AI outgrow competitors by 1.7x in revenue and 3.6x in shareholder return.
  • Benedict Sheppard, Hugo Sarrazin, Garen Kouyoumjian, and Fabricio Dore, The Business Value of Design (McKinsey). Companies that take design seriously grow faster, and most companies have no objective way to judge their own work.
  • Doug Bowman, Goodbye, Google. The designer who left after being asked to prove, with data, which of forty-one shades of blue to use, the opposite failure: measurement used to avoid judgment.

The close

  • Rick Rubin (60 Minutes). The producer who can’t play an instrument, and whose entire value is the confidence of his taste.
  • J.P. Eggers (Fortune). The NYU experiment where AI agents built startups, and the judgment that was missing without real specialists.

A founder with a tool is not a founder with a clue was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Design v ADHD
text:
Design v ADHD

ADHD is a complex and common mental disorder which changes how the person processes information, behaves, and functions in society. Common recommendations for “ADHD-friendly design” include reducing clutter, avoiding distractions, and simplifying information architecture. I argue that these suggestions do not constitute “ADHD-friendly design”, and that the real solution is more sophisticated and challenging, if not impossible, to implement.

In 2014, Ethan Zuckerman, a renowned media scholar and Internet activist, apologised for his role in inventing the Internet’s most hated marketing tool: the pop-up ad.

All of us have screwed up situations in our lives so badly that we’ve been forced to explain our actions by reminding everyone of our good intentions. It’s obvious now that what we did was a fiasco, so let me remind you that what we wanted to do was something brave and noble.

In the late 1990s, Zuckerman led a team at tripod.com — a popular service which allowed users to launch their own websites for free. Zuckerman had tried countless ways to fund the growing business until concurring that the only way to keep the company afloat was to bring in advertisers. The format invented by his team — a pop-up ad — would not only boost tripod.com’s revenue but change the Internet once and for all.

With the advent of the pop-up ad came the boom of intrusive, aggressive, and persistent advertising. The industry has weaponised our lack of attention and filled every corner of the Internet with meaningless distractions and quick rewards. Pop-ups embodied everything wrong about the advertiser-centric approach: it appeared out of thin air and demanded attention like a capricious baby, no matter what was on the user’s mind or what they were occupied with. Pop-ups reduced users to targets for the omnipresent advertisers.

The Internet today is the realm of noise and chaos. Advertisers are more vicious than their predecessors, and ads themselves have transformed to appear more organic and blend into the content until it is impossible to tell them apart. Users continue to limp around this inaccessible desert, constantly bombarded with emails and notifications informing them of special offers, keeping them up to date with what their friends have been up to, and begging them to return for more mindless entertainment.

How does someone with an already disrupted attention span find the strength to concentrate when the entire world around them is vying for their attention? How do they make decisions, resist temptations, and struggle to conform in an environment that does not suit someone like them at all?

In this article, we will discuss people with ADHD, what it means to live with this condition, and why existing design frameworks for neurodivergent users address the wrong problem.

Understanding Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorder

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects a person’s ability to concentrate and control emotions and actions. Despite being commonly associated with hyperactivity (hence the name), there are several distinct types of ADHD: hyperactive and impulsive (rather self-descriptive), inattentive (characterised by distractibility and lack of attention), and combined (the most prevalent type); each manifesting differently in each individual patient. Most commonly, people (especially adults) with ADHD have problems concentrating on the task at hand, be it a work assignment or a lengthy conversation.

MRI studies of patients with ADHD show various dysfunctions in dopamine and noradrenaline transmissions. The disorder particularly impacts the prefrontal cortex, the area of the brain involved in regulating attention, motivation, and emotion, which in turn affects the patient’s ability to concentrate, control, and shift attention.

Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder show prominent abnormalities in the inferior PFC and its connections to striatal, cerebellar, and parietal regions.

ADHD is not curable but its symptoms can be reduced and managed. There are essentially two paths to regulating attention deficit: medication and therapy. Medication is commonly prescribed to children with ADHD to address the biological mechanisms of the disorder and regulate noradrenaline and dopamine transmission in the brain. Cognitive behavioural therapy is widely used to enable self-regulation and form coping strategies. This duality, however, is a mere reflection of a wider conversation around how ADHD should be viewed and addressed. Should we side with the biomedical discourse of ADHD and choose to view it primarily as a medical category, or should we focus on addressing the flaws in a system that punishes disobedience?

It is hard to deny that ADHD affects — at times, quite severely — the patient’s ability to exist and function within complex social structures that require discipline, obedience, and compliance. Children with ADHD achieve less in school than their peers and face a higher likelihood of engaging in criminal activities. ADHD is positively correlated with anxiety and depression. Adults with ADHD struggle with employment and marital problems. Suicide rates among both children and adults with attention deficit are higher on average than in the general population.

A popular interpretation of the positivist biomedical paradigm may suggest stimulants as the most appropriate answer to curbing “undesirable behaviour”. Medication’s proven ability to improve daily functioning benefits the patient as much as an institution that will gladly drug “children into docility…in the service of a tacit project of social control”. However, acknowledging that the system obsessed with producing identical, obedient workers has little tolerance for defiance does not require viewing stimulants as a tool for enforcing cooperation. Medication is not the only way to manage the symptoms of ADHD, and it is not always the most appropriate as similar, if not more powerful, effects can be achieved with individual and systemic tools.

A more balanced take suggests viewing ADHD as the product of a complex interaction between biological and social-environmental factors. It would recognise and address the biomedical mechanisms and create opportunities for people with ADHD to function, express themselves, and realise their potential in social scenarios. This take dismisses neither medication nor therapy: it views them as valid and effective tools in their own right, but offers a reframing of what is viewed as a problem in modern society.

Take, for instance, students with ADHD, who are talkative, distracted, hyperactive. Such students are only problematic if we choose to view them as such and refuse to make the necessary adjustments to leverage, not curb, their inattentiveness. A teacher who prioritises classroom discipline is a teacher who disregards the evidence that pupils with ADHD perform significantly better when given clear instructions and expectations. The teacher’s focus on obedience and order blinds them to a multitude of opportunities to maximise student performance without disrupting the learning process: for instance, by using pupils with ADHD as peer educators. By framing attention deficit as a condition associated with some deeply problematic, anti-social, disruptive behaviours, we unwittingly set pupils with ADHD up to fail in place of a far better simple solution:

Optimal pupil performance is associated with brevity and clarity of sequences of instruction, the accompaniment of verbal instructions with visual cues and the availability of resources that pupils can refer to for reminders of direction and expectations.

The same, of course, applies to other areas of life impacted by ADHD. Building sustainable relationships, pursuing meaningful careers, enjoying the simple joys of everyday living, demand adjustments — not only from the person with ADHD but from the system itself. Reasonable accommodations are not synonymous with special treatment: they are designed to empower people who are otherwise deprived of the opportunity to function in society, not to absolve them of the need to put in effort. Such accommodations create welcoming environments where people contribute to common goals in the ways that suit them best, and where their needs and challenges are acknowledged and addressed.

ADHD v Technology

The relationship between modern technology and ADHD is complex. On the one hand, smartphones, wearable devices, and other gadgets are becoming increasingly prominent in health management and emotional regulation, complementing therapeutic and medicinal treatments with handy personalised tools. To-do lists and AI chat-bots, remote symptom tracking and online testing — adults with ADHD have plenty to choose from depending on what they wish to achieve. In addition to that, the Internet has played a big role in raising awareness of ADHD and reducing stigma around the disorder. ADHD diagnoses have increased in recent years — which, considering that women are far more likely to remain undiagnosed than men, is a positive development. Technology makes it possible for people to discover ADHD, better understand its symptoms, exchange experiences, and receive treatment.

On the other hand, the digital world is a ruthless, fast-paced, overwhelming space that is neither welcoming nor kind to people with ADHD. The rates of “Internet addiction” (which stood at 14% of children and 20% of adolescents in 2006 and has since increased) are astronomical, and neurodivergent individuals who are known to have issues with substance abuse and addiction are among the groups most affected by the phenomenon. In people with ADHD, Internet addiction is positively correlated with inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Social media is especially harmful: engineered to maximise engagement, these platforms use all sorts of tools to make it nearly impossible to quit or even reduce screen time. Excessive use of social media in particular opens the door to a range of side effects, such as low self-esteem, feelings of inadequacy and underachievement, and increased social isolation.

However, it wouldn’t be fair to blame it all on social media alone. Most modern applications are designed for engagement and employ a wide range of tools to attract and retain users. One such tool is gamification — a popular technique that uses game mechanics in non-gaming settings to reward certain behaviours and entice continuous and regular use. As research demonstrates, rewards make even the most routine tasks far more exciting, allowing users to do chores, learn languages, and socialise with ease. For people with ADHD, however, gamification is a double-edged sword: while it certainly helps make learning more enjoyable, it also exacerbates ADHD symptoms. Instant gratification makes stimulation easy to achieve, forcing the user to seek more and turning mindful gamified experiences into never-ending quests for novelty. It is worth noting that because ADHD comprises at least two major domains — inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity — the same technology that severely influences one may have little impact on the other. For example, this 2026 study found a positive correlation between the use of short video platforms and inattention but not hyperactivity-impulsivity.

The digital age has revolutionised how we create, distribute, and consume knowledge, making it far more accessible and affordable than ever before. The influx of new information and the ever-increasing speed at which new content is produced have transformed the way we live, amplified our anxieties and feelings of overwhelm. The abundance of options has further contributed to turning attention into an especially scarce and valuable resource. Today’s digital world is a terrifying place that takes users’ time and mental wellness in exchange for occasional dopamine hits. It is not designed with the neurodivergent user in mind, but it profits from their struggles: from encouraging fast, mindless interactions to enabling impulsive decisions.

Wouldn’t it be great if we could do something about this?

Why designing for ADHD is so hard

When it comes to designing for users with ADHD, recommendations commonly include reducing cognitive load, avoiding distractions, and relieving users of the need to rely on memory — solid tips that are little more than general UX principles, adjusted ever so slightly for the neurodivergent audience. These principles cannot replace a comprehensive design framework. As a complex disorder, ADHD poses multiple challenges: from social disability and academic and occupational problems to physical and psychological issues and risky behaviours. To design for ADHD means to address all these challenges at a fundamental level and, importantly, to understand why addressing them is essential in the first place.

In the book “Against Technoableism: Rethinking Who Needs Improvement”, Ashley Shew describes how most solutions are designed for people with disabilities but never with them: “[universal] design employs and imagines our bodies […] while rarely (if ever) simply asking us what we need”. What is worse, many of these solutions are built to correct or conceal disabilities rather than accommodate them. Our products, services, and environments are not simply built for the able-bodied — they force people with disabilities to adjust, to adopt particular ways of using and existing in them with the help of technology, to pretend that their disabilities are fixed or cured. Let’s medicate an inattentive student. Let’s use therapy to subdue them. Let’s agree on a design principle like “avoid clutter” in theory but allow a neurotypical middle manager to break it as they and their overlords please.

Take Bionic Reading — a method developed by Renato Casutt, a Swiss typographic designer, that emboldens the first letters of each word in a sentence to improve readability by guiding the reader’s eyes. Bionic fonts are sold for $79 per package of 10, and the company offers many other paid apps and products as well. Bionic Reading is a premium product with good advertising. It spread like wildfire in 2022, often positioned as the best possible solution for people with ADHD, dyslexia, and cognitive impairments.

Does Bionic Reading actually work? The company’s original testing method involving 12 participants (which, to the founder’s own admission, produced mixed results) does not withstand scrutiny. A real scientific test involving eye tracking on a large cohort of participants revealed that “the selective bolding of characters within words does not facilitate more efficient word identification or enhance overall reading performance in skilled adult readers”. Other tests show similar results. Bionic Reading claims that it keeps the reader’s mind focused, but in reality, it is a commercial product that tries to force a neurodivergent brain to act normally. As Daniel Lavelle at The Guardian asks: “Maybe having a wandering mind isn’t such a bad thing?” Would a better way to increase comprehension be to encourage neurodivergent people to read slowly?

So, what would it really take to design better products for people with ADHD? The process begins, unsurprisingly, with inclusion. A 2025 paper, “Towards Inclusive Guidelines for Web Design for Adults with ADHD”, describes co-designing such a framework with a panel of neurodivergent and neurotypical users. The recommendations produced by the panel varied from general UX tips (avoid complex menus, limit the number of options, keep navigation similar to other products) to ADHD-specific guidance:

  • Avoid stock photos and decorative illustrations;
  • Avoid components that may be confused with ads;
  • Restrict scrolling to vertical only;
  • Avoid non-standard hover effects and decorative animations;
  • Indicate external links and buttons.

The paper assessed these guidelines, by having two designers with ADHD put together a prototype. Nearly all suggestions yielded promising results: users with ADHD found it significantly easier to navigate the prototype designed according to these principles and discover relevant information. In the neurotypical cohort, the results were relatively moderate, although non-ADHD users, too, benefited from simplified navigation, clear information hierarchy, and other improvements. Interestingly, the only design choice that was not well received was to use the Bionic Reading method, which reportedly reduced readability in non-ADHD participants.

Does that mean that checking the boxes above will make your product ADHD-friendly?

The answer is no.

Although structured layouts and simplified navigation definitely make products easier to digest, and rewards and incentives indeed keep users with ADHD engaged, these principles alone do not amount to an ADHD-friendly framework. By narrowing the recommendations down to a short list of checkboxes, we design for people with ADHD instead of designing with them. We attempt to make them “normal” rather than empowering them to be themselves.

Product-focused approach addresses the wrong problem. It simultaneously sands down a square peg and turns a round hole into a rectangle: both parts somewhat fit one another, and everyone pretends that they are not deformed and misshapen. It does not dare to challenge the system that produces square pegs and round holes: its job is to mitigate the damage, not ask questions. Its job is to make a pop-up ad less annoying, not to find a sustainable alternative. It is to have a phone number people in wheelchairs can call for assistance instead of building accessible urban environment.

Meanwhile, designing with ADHD is the process of co-creation, of mutual learning and exchange between neurodivergent and neurotypical partners. It entails, first and foremost, transforming the environment in which the collaboration occurs. A design framework for ADHD must therefore go beyond product considerations to inform product creation itself: from establishing healthy routines and enabling productive collaboration and reflection to protecting critical decisions against corporate interference.

Under this framework, a product team could add rewards to encourage daily usage, but cannot leverage anxiety and the fear of missing out that such rewards can create. This framework would suggest the team to apply the same principles to their work as well: set short-term, achievable goals, engage and reward team members, and respect each other’s time, space, and ways of working. This framework would ensure that the product is co-designed with neurodivergent users, not tested against some vaguely defined criteria. This framework would never give rise to another pop-up ad.

Is it such a surprise that this framework does not exist?

Pop-up ads are dead. The disdain for them was so strong that by 2004, when 6.2% of all ads on the Web were pop-ups, at least 20% of all Internet users had a pop-up blocker installed. Advertisers and tech corporations they funded did not cave in until new and improved formats came along. Pop-ups did not die because the public hated them. They died because something better was on the horizon.

Pop-ups are dead, but their story, their demise, and their complicated legacy make me dread the future even more than I already do. Corporations wish to cultivate users who conform, consumers who neither demand systemic changes nor require small accommodations. In the absence of regulation and external pressure, what could possibly motivate tech giants to consider people with disabilities, let alone involve them in making important decisions?

Pop-ups are dead, but people who pushed them into existence remain in charge: not the Ethan Zuckermans who inadvertently created monsters but decision-makers who breathed life into these creatures and set them loose. So long as they remain in power, so long as growth takes priority over customer experience and care, there will be no room for human-centric thinking or accessibility. So long as they continue to reduce all users to identical numbers in a spreadsheet, any considerations that do not immediately translate into revenue will remain an afterthought, forever postponed, abandoned at the bottom of the backlog.

Two years ago, a young, moderately stressed-out PhD student wrote an article about pursuing a doctoral degree while living with ADHD. In that article, the author discussed the struggles that people with ADHD face in academia, how bureaucracy and formalities are designed, as if intentionally, to crush all hope and excitement in neurodivergent people, and how simple accommodations and small adjustments may significantly impact someone’s career. That student was optimistic about the future — his own as a neurodivergent researcher, his peers’, and the tech industry’s.

In the time since, he “toughened up”. He filled out countless ethics forms, amendment requests, and research milestone reports. He completed standardised tests, passed exams, and handed in assignments. He faced every deadline, every requirement, every expectation head-on. There was nothing that could alleviate the pressure. The system itself was not interested in changing, so he changed his ways of doing things. He succeeded at some (not all) endeavours, though in the process, lost his passion for many things he had once adored. He became timid, dull, complacent.

Back then, he was excited about things to come. Today, I no longer see him in the mirror.

What to read

  • HealthDirect. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
  • ADDA. Types of ADHD in Adults: Understanding the Differences.
  • Paul Cooper, 2008. Like Alligators Bobbing for Poodles? A Critical Discussion of Education, ADHD and the Biopsychosocial Perspective.
  • Paul Cooper, Fintan O’Regan. Educating Children with AD/HD. A Teacher’s Manual.
  • Louise C. Druedahl & Sofia Kälvemark Sporrong, 2019. A Foucauldian perspective on treating ADHD with medicine.
  • Gyöngyi Fekete & Andrés Lucero, 2019. P(L)AY ATTENTION! Co-designing for and with Children with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).
  • Ashley Shew, 2023. Against Technoableism: Rethinking Who Needs Improvement.
  • David Skidmore. Inclusion: The Dynamic of School Development.
  • Margaret D Weiss et al., 2011. The screens culture: impact on ADHD.
  • Linda Wheeler, 2010. Critique of the article by Visser and Jehan (2009): ‘ADHD: a scientific fact or a factual opinion? A critique of the veracity of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder’

About the author

Kristian Mikhel is a PhD Candidate at the University of Tasmania, a product designer and a founder of Paper and Pain, a design agency for good, an accessibility advocate, and the author of the free newsletter, “The Accessibility Apprentice”.

Design v ADHD was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: This Is The Best (And Most Romantic) Way To Get To Know Your Partner While Traveling
text:
This Is The Best (And Most Romantic) Way To Get To Know Your Partner While Traveling

I’m headed into the second year of my relationship, and I’m still getting to know my boyfriend. After more than five vacations together, I know we’re both up early, always down to explore, and very serious about trying new restaurants wherever we’re staying. But there are still stories from his past I haven’t heard and questions I haven’t thought to ask.  

That curiosity has been part of our relationship from the beginning. When we first started dating, I brought out conversation cards to help us get to know each other beyond the usual get-to-know-you icebreaker questions. Those questions gave us a place to start conversations that might not have come up on their own. They helped us get comfortable sharing more of ourselves, and the cards became something we both enjoyed. Now, sometimes he’s the one suggesting we pull out the cards.  

One thing I cherish about our relationship is how well we travel together. So, when The Skin Deep and Secrets Resorts & Spas invited us to Mexico to experience their partnership, it felt like a trip made for us. I was already familiar with The Skin Deep and its work exploring human connection, but I hadn’t realized the company also made conversation card games. The collaboration with Secrets is a limited-edition Away, Together Conversation Card Game that encourages couples to slow down and get to know each other more deeply, while on vacation.  

The resort had plenty of dining and activity options to keep us occupied, so laying on the beach and dinner became our opportunity to pull out The Skin Deep cards. We’d sit down to eat, start asking questions, and let the conversation go wherever it took us. One question stayed with me: “What is the pain in me you wish you could heal and why?” We’re still relatively early in our relationship, but we’ve already shared enough for that question to mean something. Answering it meant thinking back to the moments when we’d opened up to each other, the things we’d heard, and what had stayed with us. It made me reflect on how closely we were listening, and how much we understood about what the other person carries.

Another question that made us think: “Ten years from now, how do you think our vacations are going to differ and what do you hope remains the same?” My answer came pretty quickly: a lot more kids. He already has a six-year-old daughter, and we’ve talked about having children together, so I can definitely see more family vacations in our future. Our trips might require a little more planning and a few more suitcases, but I hope our love for travel stays the same. Even with more responsibilities and life looking different, I hope we’re still excited to see the world, experience other cultures, and try something new together. I’d love for our kids to grow up sharing that curiosity, too.

My boyfriend even admitted that The Skin Deep questions helped him be more communicative. That surprised me because, in our relationship, he’s always been willing to play along, answer, and sometimes initiate the game himself. I wouldn’t have known that opening up hadn’t always come naturally to him. Hearing that made me appreciate the habit we’d started early on even more. That’s what made this partnership feel so natural to our experience. The cards gave us a new direction to take the conversation in, and being away gave us the time to stay with the answers and really go deeper with each other. 

Going into our second year, I want us to keep making room for that curiosity at home, too. I love how well we know each other already, and I love that there’s still so much left to ask. For now, we’ll keep pulling out the cards. 

Sandy Pierre is the Branded Execution Manager at Refinery29 Unbothered and a contributing writer covering travel, lifestyle, and culture. When she’s not working on brand partnerships, she’s probably planning her next trip or curating a dinner for creatives in New York.

title: My New Fav Charlotte Tilbury Products Are On Sale For Amazon’s Holiday Beauty Haul
text:
My New Fav Charlotte Tilbury Products Are On Sale For Amazon’s Holiday Beauty Haul

As a shopping writer, there are few times when I’m actually repurchasing makeup, typically trying a revolving door of new products instead. But, there’s one beauty item that I use until the very last drop and immediately re-order: Charlotte Tilbury’s Big Lip Plumpgasm. It’s the perfect plumping lip gloss that gets me endless compliments. And now lucky for me (and you), it’s currently on sale during Amazon’s Holiday Beauty Haul Event! But there’s even more of my favorite Charlotte Tilbury goodies to score limited-time deals on.

I recently attended a Charlotte Tilbury masterclass hosted by Amazon, where we got to try tons of OG and new products while re-creating Christina Aguilera’s holiday campaign glam, taught by makeup artist Alex Rutkovskiy. While there were so many exciting products that I tried, I wanted to spotlight the ones on sale (so you can get the most bang for your buck and stock up on holiday gifts), plus share Rutkovskiy’s application tips to get the prettiest, glowiest glam this season.

Charlotte Tilbury offers a holiday cracker kit filled with the brand’s most popular Pillow Talk shade products, including the Beauty Light Wand, Lip Cheat liner, and Plumpgasm. “Pillow Talk started as one shade of lipstick,” Rutkovskiy explained, joking: “Charlotte selfishly created her personal lip color. And it’s the number one bestseller in the world.” Today, Pillow Talk has multiple iterations so everyone can enjoy it: Fair, Original, Medium, and Deep.

And right now, this makeup set is selling for under $25 on Amazon in both Pillow Talk and Super Nude, making it a great beauty kit refresh and even better stocking stuffer.

For the highlighter, which comes in seven shades (all on sale!), Rutkovskiy likes applying it to his hand first and warming it up with a brush. He then adds it to the high points of the face, like the cheekbones, nose, cupid’s bow, and chin before applying extra product with his fingertips. “It helps to layer it. It looks very healthy and glowy with more dimension. Charlotte is the queen of the glow, so we love a glowing face.” (He also called out how influencers complain about the packaging exploding in their makeup bags and purses, but that there’s a simple open-and-close twist applicator. The more you know!)

The kit also features the ultimate lip combo, IMO: Lip Cheat and Plumpgasm. Rutkovskiy taught us Charlotte Tilbury’s signature heart-shaped lip, first over-lining the cupid’s bow and center of the bottom lip. Then, you can connect the sides of your lips from the corners to the center for a lifting effect, rather than dragging down your lips.

We also applied the brand’s Matte Revolution Lipstick in Pillow Talk with a lip brush, which isn’t so much of a requirement for me. While that lip product isn’t on sale on Amazon, the creamier K.I.S.S.I.N.G Lipstick is if you want an Aguilera-esque pout.

And the final step was my Holy Grail (aka lip gloss). Speaking on Plumpgasm, Rutkovskiy said: “There’s people who hate plumping glosses and people who are obsessed with them, and there’s no one in the middle.” He added: “It’s such a beautiful formula, which combines heat and cool ingredients, so there’s pepper and mint. It’s cold and hot at the same time. And it plumps your lips in the first three minutes.” Rutkovskiy predominantly keeps the gloss at the center of the lips for extra dimension, but I definitely dowse my lips in the spicy, juicy formula, especially for late-night plans and holiday parties.

Note: If you aren’t sold on all three products in the kit, you can find the Beauty Light Wand highlighter and Plumpgasm lip gloss sold separately and on sale too!
